title: The Two Bottlenecks
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart maps two sequential obstacles standing between a new teacher and a flourishing career. The first, the Competency Bottleneck, is the time-consuming work of becoming genuinely skilled at classroom fundamentals (self-management, classroom management, student motivation, understanding how kids learn) -- a process he notes takes years even under ideal preparation and mentoring, which the US system rarely provides. The second, the Demoralization Bottleneck, hits after competency arrives: as capability grows, so does a teacher's sensitivity to how the surrounding system is broken (policy, parents, leadership, colleagues, pay, curriculum autonomy, and student circumstances all make his crowdsourced list). He validates the experience directly -- noticing dysfunction doesn't make someone a bad teacher -- and closes on the claim that thousands of experienced teachers have passed through both bottlenecks and are actively working on the systemic problems they can influence, framing the process as difficult but survivable and even, eventually, energizing.
points: The Competency Bottleneck is defined precisely: reaching Posner and Fitts's 'autonomous stage' of skill takes years even under ideal conditions, and the US teacher-prep/mentoring system varies too widely to guarantee that runway.

The Demoralization Bottleneck is framed as a consequence of competence, not a failure of it: 'as your competency increases, you gain additional bandwidth for and sensitivity to seeing the ways in which the system is broken.'

Stuart's crowdsourced list of demoralization sources (policy, parents, leaders, colleagues, pay, curriculum autonomy, student circumstances) gives the abstract bottleneck concrete, named categories rather than vague burnout language.
His explicit reframe -- 'you're not a bad teacher for noticing really hard stuff about this work' -- directly counters the guilt many competent teachers feel for recognizing systemic dysfunction.
quotes: It's just true that becoming competent at the fundamentals of teaching — self-management, classroom management, student motivation, understanding what kids are like and how they learn — is time-consuming and hard.

If you get through that one, you eventually experience a Demoralization Bottleneck. This is the moment(s) where, as your competency increases, you gain additional bandwidth for and sensitivity to seeing the ways in which the system is broken.
So look — that's an unpleasant list. I even cringed writing it. I could feel my insides tightening. I don't want to focus on the negatives, I want to focus on what I can do, what I can control.

And I guess the point of this article is that no, you're not a bad teacher for noticing really hard stuff about this work. You're probably someone who has a wrestling match every now and then with the ol' Demoralization Bottleneck.

The reality is that there are thousands of smart, passionate, wise career educators who this very day have passed through both bottlenecks. Real people like you and me are in this work and flourishing, despite its problems.
It's inner work, it's strategy, and it's action wisely taken to improve the things we think we have a shot at improving. And you know what? I think there's a way for it to even be fun.
